title: My Doc-Site
text: My Doc-Site A scaffold for knowledge bases you curate yourself, rendered as a fast, dependency-free static site. You own the structure and the summaries; because the rendered HTML is the source, Claude writes and cross-links the pages for you. No build step, no pip , no npm — just Python's standard library and a folder of HTML. You are reading the site right now. Every page here is both the manual for the scaffold and a live demonstration of how it lays out content. Start here Guide — install, run, the conventions, and why the scaffold is shaped this way. Recipes — copy-paste how-tos for the common changes (add a page, add a tab, group the sidebar). How it works in one paragraph Navigation is filesystem-driven . Each directory under docs/pages/ becomes a top tab; each .html file becomes a page. You author content inside a <main class="doc-body"> block, then run the wrap script — it regenerates the chrome (header, sidebar, breadcrumbs, on-this-page TOC, footer) from the current file tree. A tiny stdlib dev server live-reloads the browser as you edit. Branding lives in docs/_site.json ; per-tab nav lives in docs/pages/<tab>/_tab.json . That's the whole system.

title: A loose page
text: A loose page This file lives directly in demo/ , so it shows up as a page near the top of the sidebar — a sibling of the Guides and Extras dividers below it. Why it's here Pages and folders coexist at every level. No folder is required to hold a page.

title: Extra one
text: Extra one This page is inside demo/extras/ , a folder with no index.html . So in the sidebar, “Extras” is a plain, non-clickable label — a pure divider — while its pages still list underneath. Contrast with Guides “Guides” was clickable because it had an index; “Extras” isn't because it doesn't.

title: Extra two
text: Extra two A second page under the index-less Extras divider. Note Add a folder, add pages, refresh — that's the whole workflow.

title: First guide
text: First guide An ordinary page inside the Guides divider. Note Its sidebar label and this page's title both come from the <title> / <h1> .

title: Guides
text: Guides This folder has an index.html — so “Guides” in the sidebar is clickable and opens this very page. That's the role of a folder's index: its default page. Contents Below this divider you'll find First guide and a further-nested Nested divider.

title: Deep page
text: Deep page Three levels down and still zero config. That's the bottom Nothing special needed to reach here — just nested folders.

title: Nested (depth 3)
text: Nested (depth 3) Folders nest as deep as you like. This is demo/guides/nested/ — a divider inside a divider. It has its own index.html , so it's clickable too. Depth The breadcrumb above shows the full path; the sidebar auto-expands to the active page.

title: Demo — built by dropping a folder
text: Demo — built by dropping a folder This entire tab was created by dropping docs/pages/demo/ into the repo — no _tab.json , no required index.html . The sidebar on the left is a live mirror of the folder tree. Open each item and compare it to the structure below. The folder behind this tab demo/ ├── index.html ← you are here (this tab's default page) ├── a-loose-page.html ← a page, sibling of the folders ├── guides/ ← folder WITH index.html → clickable divider │ ├── index.html │ ├── first-guide.html │ └── nested/ ← nests to any depth │ ├── index.html │ └── deep-page.html └── extras/ ← folder WITHOUT index.html → plain divider ├── one.html └── two.html What to notice A folder = a divider. Its index.html (if present) is the divider's clickable default page. Loose .html files are pages alongside the folders. It recurses to any depth. Delete this folder anytime — it's just a demo.

title: Conventions
text:
Conventions The operating rules for this scaffold. Read once, apply mechanically thereafter. 1. The filesystem IS the nav Every directory under docs/pages/ becomes a top tab. Inside a tab, the folder tree is mirrored recursively into the sidebar — you never maintain a central nav list, and nothing needs an index.html . Drop a folder docs/pages// with any .html inside → a new tab X appears, opening to its first page. No config, no index required. A subfolder becomes a collapsible divider ; the loose .html files in a folder are pages that sit alongside its subfolders, at every level. An index.html is optional : if a folder has one, it's that folder's clickable default page (the tab or divider opens to it); if not, the divider is just a label. Move or rename a file/folder → its nav entry and URL follow. Recurses to any depth: tab → divider → page , mirrored straight from the filesystem. So dropping a nested folder of HTML "just works" with zero config. Directories and files whose names start with _ or . are skipped by the scanner — that's how _lib/ , _tab.json , and _site.json stay out of the nav. 2. _tab.json is for overrides only Each tab may carry a docs/pages//_tab.json . It never adds pages — it only adjusts how discovered pages are presented. All fields are optional: Field Effect label Tab text in the header (default: title-cased directory name). key CSS accent class for the tab (default: directory name). landing Page the tab opens to, relative to the tab dir (default: index.html , else the first page). order_priority Smaller = further left in the tab strip (default: 100). sections Curated sidebar groups with explicit order/labels (see §6). Omit (the default) to mirror the folder tree recursively. external_layout true = the tab's pages own their chrome; the wrap script leaves them alone (see §10). If alphabetical order is fine and the directory name title-cases well, skip the file entirely. 3. Two-to-five tabs is the sweet spot One tab feels undercooked; six or more crowds the bar. Pick 2–5 top-level directories. Tab order is by order_priority (then directory name) — set it explicitly in each _tab.json rather than relying on the default. 4. The root landing is docs/index.html The bare URL / serves docs/index.html directly — there is no redirect plugin and no magic. Edit that file to be your welcome page, or replace its body with a link hub. It is wrapped with the same chrome as every other page (its breadcrumb root is the site name; its right-TOC is suppressed). 5. Author inside
Every page you write is a normal HTML document whose authored content lives in a single
…
block, with a in the head. The wrap script extracts exactly that block and re-renders the full page around it. Rules that make a page behave: The <title> sets the browser title and the sidebar/breadcrumb label. Don't add the site-name suffix yourself — the wrapper does. Give section headings an id ( <h2 id="overview"> ). The on-this-page TOC is built from <h2 id> and <h3 id> . Page-specific <style> in the head and trailing <script> blocks are preserved across re-wraps. 6. The chrome is baked — automatically while you serve The header/sidebar/breadcrumbs/TOC aren't in your authored files; they're generated around your <main> block. The dev server does this for you : it bakes on startup and re-bakes on every change, so dropping or editing files "just works" — no manual step. (Disable with NO_AUTOWRAP=1 ./run_dev.sh if you want manual control.) When the server isn't running (e.g. in CI, or before committing), bake manually: python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py It is idempotent and only writes files that actually changed: running it twice produces no further change, and it won't double-escape titles or stack footers. A page is recognised by its <main class="doc-body"> block, so it's safe to repeat. Curated sidebar sections (optional) By default the sidebar mirrors the folder tree (§1) — no config. When you want explicit labels or a pinned order, add sections to _tab.json . Each section names a directory (relative to the tab) and may pin an order of file stems: "sections": [ {"label": "Getting Started", "dir": "getting-started", "key": "guide"}, {"label": "Reference", "dir": "reference", "key": "guide", "order": ["concepts", "api"]} ] A section with "dir": "" points at the tab root itself — that's how a flat tab pins a custom page order, as both tabs in this site do. Drop sections and the tab reverts to the zero-config recursive mirror. 7. assets/ and _lib/ are invisible to the nav The scanner only looks under docs/pages/ , and skips _ / . names. So docs/assets/ (CSS/JS/images), docs/_lib/ (the engine), and the _*.json config files never become tabs. Reference assets with a path relative to the page; the wrap script computes the correct ../ prefix for the layout's own asset links. 8. Cross-page links use relative paths Link between pages with ordinary relative hrefs ending in .html : <a href="../recipes/add-a-tab.html">Add a tab</a> When you move a directory, cross-boundary links break. There's no strict-build checker shipped, so grep for the old path after a move: grep -rn 'old-folder/' docs/pages/ . 9. Branding lives in docs/_site.json Site name, tagline, footer, and logo target are read from _site.json by the layout and nav code — never hardcode them in _lib/ . Change the name there, re-wrap, and the logo, <title> suffix, breadcrumb root, and footer all update together. Set base_url (the public URL the site is published at) to switch on absolute OpenGraph tags — og:url and og:image — so shared links unfurl with a preview card. Left empty, the relative <meta name="description"> and og:title / og:description tags are still emitted; only the absolute ones are skipped. 10. external_layout for self-chromed pages Some pages own their full markup — a Reveal.js deck, a generated report, an embedded app. Mark their tab with "external_layout": true in _tab.json ; the wrap script then skips that tab entirely, leaving its HTML untouched while the tab still appears in the header. See Recipes → Include an HTML deck .

title: Guide
text: Guide You are reading a doc-site that documents itself. The site you are browsing right now is the template — every page is both the manual for the scaffold and a live demonstration of how it organizes content. What this template gives you Zero dependencies. Pure Python standard library — no pip , no npm , no build step. If you have python3 , you can run it. Filesystem-driven nav. Each directory under docs/pages/ becomes a tab; each .html file becomes a page. Drop a file in, it appears. Author content, not chrome. You write a <main class="doc-body"> block; the wrap script regenerates the header, sidebar, breadcrumbs, on-this-page TOC, and footer for you. Live-reload dev server. A stdlib HTTP server watches the tree and pushes a browser reload over Server-Sent Events when anything changes. One config file for branding ( docs/_site.json ) and one per tab for nav ( _tab.json ). Where to go next Installation — get the template running locally. Quick Start — make your first edits. Why this pattern — the rationale in one page. Conventions — the operating rules you'll reference daily. Recipes for common tasks live under the Recipes tab.

title: Installation
text: Installation There is no environment to install This is the headline feature: zero dependencies . The dev server and the wrap script are written entirely against the Python standard library, so there is no pip install , no conda environment, no npm , and no build step . Nothing to pin, nothing to keep in sync, nothing to rot — if a machine has python3 , it can serve this site, today and in three years. Concretely, getting from clone to a running site is two commands: git clone https://github.com/jianzhou0420/htmlkb.git my-docs cd my-docs && ./run_dev.sh For contrast, the generator-based predecessor of this scaffold required a conda create plus pip install -r requirements.txt (MkDocs, the theme, and several nav/redirect plugins) — and broke when a transitive dependency drifted. That entire class of setup and upkeep is gone. Prerequisites Python 3.8+ on your PATH — the only requirement. The dev server and wrap script are pure standard library, so there is nothing to pip install . If your interpreter isn't named python3 , point at it with PYTHON=/path/to/python ./run_dev.sh . Git — for cloning, and recommended for version-controlling your own content. Clone git clone https://github.com/jianzhou0420/htmlkb.git my-docs cd my-docs Or use the "Use this template" button on GitHub to create your own repo from this one. There are no submodules to recurse and no environment to create. Serve locally ./run_dev.sh This launches the stdlib live-reload server ( docs/_lib/_serve.py ) on http://0.0.0.0:8002 . It serves docs/ directly — there is no compiled output. Edit any file and the browser reloads within about half a second. Override host, port, or poll interval: ./run_dev.sh 9000 # custom port HOST=127.0.0.1 ./run_dev.sh # bind localhost only INTERVAL=1.0 ./run_dev.sh # slower file-watch poll (default 0.5s) Deploy Because the site is the static output, deploying is just copying docs/ to any static host (GitHub Pages, Netlify, S3, nginx). The _lib/ Python is only used at authoring time; you can exclude it from the upload, or leave it — browsers ignore .py files. Uninstall Delete the clone. No system-wide state is created. Troubleshooting "python3: command not found" — install Python 3, or edit run_dev.sh to point at your interpreter. Port already in use — pass a different port: ./run_dev.sh 9000 . A page shows no sidebar or wrong title — re-run the wrap script: python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py . See Conventions § Bake the chrome . Edits don't reload — the watcher ignores dotfiles and __pycache__ ; make sure you're editing a tracked .html / .css / .js file under docs/ .

title: Quick Start
text:
Quick Start Assumes you have installed the template and are running ./run_dev.sh . 1. Rename the site Open docs/_site.json and edit the branding: { "site_name": "My Project Docs", "tagline": "Short tagline", "footer": "My Project Docs", "logo_href": "index.html" } The site_name drives the header logo, the suffix, and (unless you override footer ) the footer text. After editing, re-bake the chrome so every page picks up the change: python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py 2. Edit the landing page The root URL / serves docs/index.html . Open it and replace the content inside <main class="doc-body">…</main> with your project's welcome text. Leave the <main> wrapper in place — the wrap script keys off it. 3. Add content Add a page Create an HTML file inside a tab directory with a <title> and a <main class="doc-body"> block: cat > docs/pages/guide/architecture.html <<'EOF' <!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"> <title>Architecture

Architecture

Overview

…

EOF python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py Refresh the browser — the page appears in the Guide sidebar. Headings with an id attribute (

) automatically populate the on-this-page TOC on the right. Control the order By default sidebar pages sort alphabetically (with index.html first). To pin a custom order, list the file stems in the tab's docs/pages/guide/_tab.json : "order": ["index", "installation", "architecture", "quick-start", "why", "conventions"] Add a tab Create a new directory under docs/pages/ with at least an index.html : mkdir docs/pages/reference # author docs/pages/reference/index.html with a
block python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py A Reference tab appears. See Recipes → Add a tab for labels, ordering, and sidebar sections. 4. Ship There's no build. Copy docs/ to any static host. See Installation → Deploy . Next Why this pattern — understand the tradeoffs before deviating. Conventions — the full ruleset. Recipes — common tasks with worked examples.

title: Why this pattern
text: Why this pattern The problem it solves A conventional documentation site leans on a generator (MkDocs, Docusaurus, Hugo) plus a plugin ecosystem. That buys you a lot, but it also means a toolchain to install, a config to learn, a build step to run, and a dependency tree that drifts and breaks between machines and over time. For a personal, long-lived knowledge base you curate — where you shape the structure, Claude writes the pages, and you read the result — that overhead earns little and costs upkeep. This scaffold takes the opposite bet: the rendered HTML is the source , and the only tooling is a few hundred lines of Python standard library. What this scaffold does instead Concern How it's handled Navigation _lib/_nav.py scans docs/pages/ . Each directory is a tab; each .html file is a page. No central nav list. Page chrome _lib/_layout.py renders one shared shell; _lib/_wrap_handwritten.py bakes it onto every authored <main> . Change the layout once, re-wrap, done. Per-tab tweaks An optional _tab.json per tab overrides label, ordering, and sidebar grouping — local to that tab, no global config. Live preview _lib/_serve.py : stdlib HTTP + mtime polling + Server-Sent Events. No watchdog, no websocket library. Dependencies None. python3 is the whole requirement. Result: adding content is a one-step action — create an HTML file, run the wrap script, commit. The tradeoffs — honest version You write HTML, not Markdown. No Markdown-to-HTML convenience, no fenced-code niceties out of the box. For an LLM author this is a non-issue — Claude emits HTML as readily as Markdown — but a human typing pages by hand will feel it. No plugin ecosystem. Search, diagrams, math, versioning — anything a mature generator ships as a plugin, you'd add yourself. The header has a placeholder search button that's intentionally a stub. The wrap step is manual. Chrome isn't regenerated on save; you run _wrap_handwritten.py after structural changes. The dev server reloads content live, but new pages/tabs need a wrap to get their chrome. You own the CSS. Theming is a single assets/style.css you edit directly, not a configured theme. More control, more rope. When this pattern shines Knowledge bases you curate — you shape the structure; Claude writes the HTML directly into pages/ ; you read the result. Long-lived personal sites where "still builds in three years with zero dependency rot" matters more than a rich plugin set. Air-gapped or minimal environments — if it has Python, it runs. When it doesn't Human-authored docs where Markdown ergonomics and a copy-button-on-code-blocks experience matter — reach for MkDocs Material. You need full-text search, i18n, or versioned docs today — those come free in mature generators and would be real work here. A large team that wants a single auditable nav file and a CI-enforced build contract.

title: Add a page
text:
Add a page Minimum steps Create an HTML file inside a tab directory. The only requirements are a and a <main class="doc-body"> block: cat > docs/pages/guide/new-page.html <<'EOF' <!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"> <title>New page

New page

…

EOF With ./run_dev.sh running, the page appears in the Guide sidebar automatically — the dev server bakes the header, sidebar, breadcrumbs, TOC, and footer for you. (If the server isn't running, bake once with python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py .) Controlling position By default, new pages sort alphabetically (with index.html first). To pin a slot, add the file's stem to the order list in the tab's _tab.json section: "order": ["index", "installation", "new-page", "quick-start", "why", "conventions"] Stems not listed in order fall to the bottom, alphabetically. The title and the on-this-page TOC The sidebar label and breadcrumb come from the tag (the site-name suffix is added for you — don't type it). The on-this-page TOC on the right is built from headings that carry an id : <h2 id="overview">Overview</h2> <h3 id="details">Details</h3> Headings without an id are skipped by the TOC. Linking to it From another page in the same tab: <a href="new-page.html">New page</a> From a different tab: <a href="../guide/new-page.html">New page</a>

title: Add a tab
text: Add a tab Minimum steps Just drop a folder containing one or more .html pages (each with a <main class="doc-body"> block) under docs/pages/ — no index.html and no _tab.json required : mkdir docs/pages/reference # author one or more pages, e.g. docs/pages/reference/overview.html With ./run_dev.sh running, a Reference tab appears automatically (the dev server bakes the chrome for you). If the server isn't running, bake once with python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py . The tab opens to its first page; any subfolders become collapsible sidebar dividers, recursively (see Conventions §1 ). A tab with no serveable .html at all is silently skipped. Everything below is optional — add a _tab.json only when you want to override the auto behaviour. Controlling tab order Tabs sort by order_priority (smaller is further left), then by directory name. Set it in the new tab's _tab.json : { "label": "Reference", "order_priority": 30 } Giving the tab a non-slug label The directory name determines the URL ( /pages/reference/... ). The label shown in the header defaults to the title-cased directory name; override it with label : { "label": "API Reference", "order_priority": 30 } Result: the URL stays at pages/reference/... , the tab reads "API Reference". Picking an accent color The key field selects a CSS accent class from docs/assets/style.css (e.g. guide , designdoc , capability , research , architecture ). Pick one, or add your own accent variables to the stylesheet: { "label": "API Reference", "key": "architecture", "order_priority": 30 } Giving the tab a sidebar A tab only renders sidebar entries for pages inside its sections . For a flat tab (files directly in the tab dir), add one section pointing at the tab root with "dir": "" : { "label": "API Reference", "order_priority": 30, "sections": [ {"label": "Reference", "dir": "", "key": "architecture"} ] } For a tab organized into subdirectories, either list a section per subdir or omit sections to auto-discover them. See Sidebar sections & sub-sections . Removing a tab Delete the directory and re-run the wrap script. Any links that pointed into it will now 404 — grep for the old path to find them: grep -rn 'pages/reference/' docs/ .

title: Include an HTML deck
text:
Include an HTML deck Rendered slide decks (Reveal.js, Marp, PowerPoint → HTML export) and other self-contained pages own their own full markup. You don't want the wrap script injecting the site chrome into the middle of a deck. The mechanism for that is external_layout . How it works A tab marked "external_layout": true in its _tab.json still appears in the header, but the wrap script skips every page inside it — the files are served exactly as authored. Use this for any tab whose pages are not
documents. Steps Create the tab directory and drop your decks in: mkdir docs/pages/decks cp ~/exports/q1-review.html docs/pages/decks/index.html cp ~/exports/pitch.html docs/pages/decks/pitch.html Mark it external in docs/pages/decks/_tab.json : { "label": "Decks", "key": "research", "landing": "index.html", "order_priority": 40, "external_layout": true, "sections": [] } Re-run the wrap script. It reports the decks tab as skipped (by design) and leaves those files byte-for-byte intact: python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py Clicking the Decks tab opens index.html as-is; the deck controls its own navigation. Linking to a deck from a normal page

Watch the Q1 review deck.

Notes Source files ( .pptx , .key ) don't belong under docs/ — they won't render and they bloat the repo. Keep them elsewhere and commit only the exported HTML. Embedded media in a deck inflates page weight; the dev server's no-cache headers mean large decks reload slowly. Keep them lean where you can. The external_layout flag is per tab , not per page. If you want one normal page plus some self-chromed pages, put the self-chromed ones in their own tab.

title: Recipes
text: Recipes Task-oriented how-tos. Each recipe is short and focused on one change you might make to your doc-site. Add a page Add a tab Rename a tab Include an HTML deck Sidebar sections & sub-sections For the principles behind these recipes, see Conventions .

title: Rename a tab
text: Rename a tab Two different things people call "rename a tab": A. Change the label, keep the URL The label shown in the header is separate from the directory name (which drives the URL). To change only the label, edit the tab's _tab.json : { "label": "Developer Handbook" } Re-run python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py . No files move, existing links work, done. B. Change the URL too You want the URL to change from /pages/guide/... to /pages/handbook/... . Rename the directory: git mv docs/pages/guide docs/pages/handbook Then: Update any cross-tab links that point into the renamed directory. Find them: grep -rn 'pages/guide/' docs/ grep -rn '\.\./guide/' docs/pages/ Re-run the wrap script so the new tab's pages get fresh chrome and breadcrumbs: python3 docs/_lib/_wrap_handwritten.py If you need to preserve old bookmarks, drop a tiny redirect stub at the old path (a plain HTML <meta http-equiv="refresh"> page), since there's no redirect plugin. Rule of thumb: rename the label (A) freely; rename the URL (B) only when you really need to.

title: Sidebar sections & sub-sections
text: Sidebar sections & sub-sections The left sidebar of a tab is built from its sections (declared in _tab.json ) plus the actual subdirectory tree on disk. This recipe shows the three shapes you'll reach for. Flat tab, one section Files live directly in the tab directory, no subfolders. Point one section at the tab root with "dir": "" and pin the order. Both tabs in this site use this shape: { "label": "Guide", "sections": [ {"label": "Guide", "dir": "", "key": "guide", "order": ["index", "installation", "quick-start", "why", "conventions"]} ] } Grouped by subdirectory Organize files into subfolders and give each one a section. The section's dir is relative to the tab: docs/pages/knowledge-base/ ├── getting-started/ index.html, setup.html ├── benchmarks/ vln.html, eqa.html, vla.html └── methods/ navgpt.html, mapgpt.html { "label": "Knowledge Base", "sections": [ {"label": "Getting Started", "dir": "getting-started", "key": "guide"}, {"label": "Benchmarks", "dir": "benchmarks", "key": "guide"}, {"label": "Methods", "dir": "methods", "key": "guide", "order": ["navgpt", "mapgpt"]} ] } Nested subdirectories are discovered recursively: a subfolder with its own index.html becomes a collapsible group whose label is that page's title; without an index.html it becomes a non-clickable group label. The group auto-expands when it contains the active page. Auto-discovery (no sections at all) Omit sections from _tab.json (or skip the file entirely) and the scanner creates one section per immediate subdirectory, alphabetically, each labelled from the title-cased folder name. Good for "just works" tabs where you don't care about ordering or custom labels. Sections vs. subfolders — which to use One flat section when the tab has a handful of peer pages. Subfolders + curated sections when you want named groups, control over order, and short, stable per-group URLs. Auto-discovery when the structure is still in flux and you don't want to maintain a config. Because grouping is expressed in _tab.json and on the filesystem — not in the page content — you can regroup the sidebar by editing one file and re-running the wrap script, without touching any page.
